words.g: and by the ones sent forth

1.sense: Five oath-clauses open the surah and not one of them names its subject. The first swears by feminine plurals sent out, and ʿurfan reads either as a horse's mane, strand following strand, or as maʿrūf, sent for good. Nothing is sworn to yet; the sentence does not finish until verse seven.

notes.t: ʿUrf is the mane along a horse's neck, and the accusative carries the picture of things arriving in a continuous line rather than singly. The other reading takes the same word as maʿrūf, kindness, so the sending is for good.

The exegetes divide over what the five clauses swear by: the winds, the angels, or the messengers who carry revelation. Some split the set, reading the earlier clauses of the winds and the later ones of the angels. The disagreement is old and was never settled.
notes.src: at-Tabari and al-Qurtubi record the winds and the angels side by side, without a decisive report

notes.t: The Qur'an opens several surahs this way, with a run of unnamed feminine plurals sworn by and the answer withheld until the run is complete: the scatterers, the chargers.
Abdullah ibn Masʿud said they were with the Prophet ﷺ in a cave at Mina when Al-Mursalat came down, and that he was taking it from the Prophet's mouth as he recited, when a snake came out at them.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, Book of Tafsir, from Abdullah ibn Masʿud

links.why: the same kind of opening, unnamed feminine plurals sworn by before the sentence lands
another oath series of five, and the same withheld subject

2.sense: The second clause turns the sending violent. ʿAsf is the tearing wind, and the bare verbal noun after the participle doubles it: storming a storming. The fā' at the front makes this the next thing the same agents do, not a new set of agents.

notes.t: The noun from this root, ʿasf, is the dry husk a gale strips off a stalk. The Qur'an uses it of grain with its chaff, and of an army left like straw that has been eaten.
Three of the five clauses end in a cognate accusative, ʿasfan, nashran and farqan: the verbal noun repeated after its own participle. It intensifies rather than adds information.

links.why: the scattering winds sworn by with the same doubled construction

3.sense: Nashr is the opening out of what was folded: a cloth unrolled, cloud pulled across the sky, a written page laid flat. The same root gives nushūr, the raising of the dead. The word already leans toward what the oath is about to promise.

notes.t: The Qur'an ends a verse about winds driving cloud to a dead land with the words ‘such is the raising’, joining this root to resurrection directly.
The same verb is used in the passive of the record scrolls: and when the pages are spread open.
Nashr covers three things at once in Arabic: spreading, scattering, and reviving. The clause does not choose between them.

links.why: the winds stirring cloud and spreading it across the sky as He wills

4.sense: The fourth clause names the work the others were doing: cutting truth from falsehood so that the two no longer sit together. The root is the one behind furqān, the criterion. The oath and the thing sworn to are being built out of a single idea.

notes.t: The same root names the Qur'an itself, al-Furqān, sent down to a servant as a warning, and names Badr the day of criterion, the day the two forces met.
Farq is a parting made by a cut. The Qur'an uses this very verb of the sea divided for the Children of Israel, water opened and held apart.
Farq here and fasl at verse thirteen are two roots for one act. The oath is sworn by separators; what it swears to is the day of separation.

links.why: the same act under its other root, the Day of Decision the oath is sworn about

5.sense: The fifth and last clause. Ilqā' is to throw a thing down so it lands where it was aimed, and what is thrown is dhikr, the reminder. Whatever the earlier clauses carried, this one carries revelation to a heart, which is why many read the whole series as the angels.

notes.t: The Qur'an uses this same verb of Allah casting the spirit of His command upon whom He wills among His servants, to warn of the Day of Meeting.
Dhikr is both the act of remembering and the thing that causes it, and the Qur'an calls itself by the word. The clause says what is cast and not to whom; verse six supplies the purpose instead.

links.why: the trustworthy spirit bringing the revelation down onto the heart

6.sense: Two purposes for the reminder, set side by side. ʿUdhr here is not an excuse offered but an excuse removed, so that nobody can say he was never told; nudhr is the warning itself. The first looks back at the one who receives it, the second forward at what is coming.

notes.t: Messengers are sent bearing good news and warning so that people should have no argument against Allah after them. That is what ʿudhran states in one word.
The root of ʿudhran returns at verse thirty-six, where no leave is given for the deniers to excuse themselves. What the sending took away then cannot be produced later.

links.why: the other end of the same root, an excuse offered and not heard

7.sense: The oath reaches its answer. Everything sworn by in the first six verses stands behind one short clause: what you are promised will happen. Wāqiʿ is the participle of falling, an event that comes down rather than a statement that is merely true.

notes.t: Adh-Dhariyat opens on the same kind of oath and closes it with the same word: what you are promised is true, and the recompense is lawāqiʿ, bound to occur.
The lām on lawāqiʿ is the lām that marks an oath's answer, and innamā restricts: not merely that it will happen, but that this and nothing else is the case.

links.why: the Event named by this participle, al-Wāqiʿa, and given a whole surah

8.sense: The first of four when-clauses describing the day just promised. Tams is the wiping away of a trace until there is nothing left to read: writing rubbed off, a road effaced by sand. The stars are not said to fall but to lose the light that made them useful.

notes.t: The Qur'an says the stars were set for finding the way through the darknesses of land and sea. Blotting them out takes the marks from the traveller before the rest of the scene begins.
This verb is Musa's word in his prayer against Pharaoh's wealth, and it is used of faces effaced. In both places what is removed is a feature, not a body.

links.why: the same stars under a different verb, going dull and dropping

9.sense: The second clause. Farj is a gap between two things, and the passive says the sky is given one. What is undone here is exactly what Qaf describes as the sky's present condition.

notes.t: Qaf tells the deniers to look at the sky above them, built and adorned, with no rifts in it at all, furūj being this verse's word in the plural. The present tightness is what makes the opening an event.
Furijat is passive throughout: the sky does not open, it is opened. All four clauses of this section are built the same way, with no agent named.

links.why: the sky giving way, described as listening to its Lord

10.sense: The third clause. Nasf is what a winnower does, tossing grain up so the light part blows off. The mountains are not toppled where they stand; they are lifted and scattered.

notes.t: Asked what will become of the mountains, the Prophet ﷺ is told to answer with this verb: my Lord will blow them away utterly, and leave the ground a bare level plain.
The same verb is used of the calf Musa burned and then scattered into the sea. In both places the thing is destroyed by being dispersed rather than broken.

links.why: the same mountains set firm and towering, in the surah's own list of favours

11.sense: The fourth clause turns from the sky and the earth to the messengers themselves. Uqqitat is built on waqt, an appointed time, so they are brought to the hour set for them. The focus shifts from things breaking to a court assembling.

notes.t: The Qur'an describes the day Allah gathers the messengers and asks what answer they were given. That gathering is the appointment this verse sets.
The hamza at the front of uqqitat stands in for a wāw; the root is w-q-t, which also gives mīqāt, an appointed time and place.

links.why: the Day of Decision named a mīqāt, the noun from this verse's root

12.sense: A question thrown into the middle of the scene with nobody named to answer it. Ta'jīl is the setting of a term, and the passive leaves out who set it. The question is not about ignorance; it is the pause before the answer lands.

notes.t: Ajal is a span with an end fixed to it. The verb says the messengers' appointment was held to a particular day, not that it was forgotten.
The Qur'an says every community has a term, and when that term comes they can neither put it back by an hour nor bring it forward.

13.sense: The answer, two words long. Fasl is the cut that separates one thing from another, and so also the verdict that settles a case. The day is named by what happens on it: the parties are divided and the matter is closed.

notes.t: An-Naba' names the same day and calls it a mīqāt, an appointed time, which answers verse twelve's question with the noun from verse eleven's verb.
As-Saffat has the phrase said to the deniers on the day itself: this is the Day of Decision, the one you used to call a lie.

links.why: the same naming repeated at the far end of the surah, with the gathering assembled

14.sense: A formula the Qur'an uses to say that a named thing lies past the reach of the one addressed. The name was already given in the verse before, and the question says the name is not the same as knowing. What follows is not a definition but a sentence passed.

notes.t: Wa-mā adrāka occurs thirteen times in the Qur'an, and everywhere else the next verse supplies the answer: Saqar, the Striking, the Night of Decree. Here alone the naming came first, in the verse before, and what follows the question is the woe.

The imperfect form of the same question, wa-mā yudrīka, is used three times and is never answered: the nearness of the Hour, and whether a man will purify himself. The past-tense form promises an answer; the present-tense form withholds one.
The question is doubled over the Day of Recompense in Al-Infitar, which is the only place the Qur'an asks it twice about the same thing.

links.why: the same question put about the Striking, with the answer following at once

15.sense: The refrain enters for the first time, directly after the day has been named and left unexplained. Wayl is a cry of ruin rather than a sentence with a verb in it. It will return nine more times, once after each panel of the surah.

notes.t: The refrain falls ten times here. Counted as a repeated line, only Ar-Rahman's runs more often, thirty-one times, and both turn on the same verb, kadhdhaba, to call a thing a lie.
Mukadhdhibīn is not a word for the ignorant. The form is intensive and takes an object: those who received something and declared it false.
The same sentence stands outside this surah twice, in At-Tur with a fā' in front of it and in Al-Mutaffifin unchanged.

links.why: the Qur'an's other great refrain, built on the same verb but put as a question

16.sense: The argument turns to history. A question shaped to expect assent, because the record of ruined nations was already in front of the listeners, in the wreckage along their own trade roads. Alam makes it a challenge rather than an enquiry.

notes.t: The Qur'an points the Meccans at generations destroyed before them, better established in the land than they were, and says elsewhere that their own likes have already been destroyed.
Awwalīn, the earliest peoples, returns at verse thirty-eight, where the same peoples are gathered rather than destroyed.

links.why: the ruined nations named, ʿAd and Iram of the pillars

17.sense: The tense moves. The destruction of the first peoples is stated as finished; the sending of the later ones after them is stated as still running. Thumma marks the gap between the two, and the imperfect verb leaves the second half open.

notes.t: Nutbiʿuhum is imperfect where nuhliki sat inside a question about the past. What is described is not closed history but a rule still in force.
Az-Zukhruf makes the same move: We destroyed men stronger than these in grip, and the case of the former peoples has passed into a proverb.

18.sense: The rule stated flat. Kadhālika gathers the two halves of the preceding verses into one practice, and mujrimīn names who it falls on. Jurm is the cutting of fruit from a tree, so the criminal is the one who severs what should have held.

notes.t: The Qur'an states the same rule with the same adverb in Al-Aʿraf and Yunus: thus do We repay the guilty.
Mujrimīn returns at verse forty-six, where the deniers are told to eat and enjoy a little because that is what they are. The word holds both ends of the surah's case against them.
Kadhālika nafʿalu here has its match at verse forty-four, innā kadhālika najzī al-muhsinīn. One adverb serves both parties.

links.why: the same ‘thus’ turned toward the doers of good

19.sense: The woe on the historical panel. What was shown was a record rather than a threat, ruins a caravan could walk through. The refrain fixes the ruin to those who have that in front of them and still call the warning false.

notes.t: Each occurrence takes its force from the passage it closes. Here that passage is an argument from wreckage, not from anything unseen.
The Qur'an tells the Meccans plainly that they pass by the ruined town morning and night, and asks whether they will not use their minds.

20.sense: The second question turns from other people's ruins to the listener's own body. Mā' mahīn is water that carries no standing; the adjective is the one used of a man held weak and of no account. Whoever made a person out of that can do the rest of what has been promised.

notes.t: The same two words stand in As-Sajda, where the making of a man's offspring from a despised fluid sits between his creation from clay and the breathing of the spirit into him.
Mahīn, from m-h-n, is the opposite of what is prized. The verse does not soften it; the argument turns on the distance between the material and the result.

links.why: the same question put as a command, let man look at what he was made from

21.sense: The fluid is moved to a place built to hold it. Qarār is where a thing settles and stays; makīn is firm, established, the adjective of a position that cannot be shaken. Mahīn in the verse before and makīn here rhyme against each other, the worthless set into the secure.

notes.t: Al-Mu'minun uses the identical phrase for the same stage, a drop placed in a firm lodging, and then lists what is made from it.
Makīn comes from makāna, place and standing together. The Qur'an uses it of a person of rank as readily as of a physical position.

links.why: the stages that follow the lodging, each one made out of the last

22.sense: The lodging has a term attached to it. Qadar is both a fixed amount and a fixed span, and maʿlūm says it is known, not by the one addressed but by the one who set it. Nothing in the process is left loose.

notes.t: Abdullah ibn Masʿud reported the Prophet ﷺ describing the making of a person in the mother in set periods of forty days each, and then the sending of the angel. The measure this verse calls known is given there as a count of days.
notes.src: Bukhari, Book of the Beginning of Creation, and Muslim, Book of Qadar, from Abdullah ibn Masʿud

notes.t: Al-Hajj sets out the same stages and draws the same conclusion from them, addressing people who are in doubt about being raised.
Qadarin plants the root that verse twenty-three then uses twice. The argument turns on one word: a measure known, and the One who measures.

23.sense: The verb takes up the noun from the verse before and turns it into an act. Fa-niʿma is a formula of praise that holds its subject to the end, so the sentence closes on al-qādirūn. The one who measured a person into being is the one able to measure him back.

notes.t: The word is read both qadarnā and qaddarnā among the canonical readings, the sense moving between determining and measuring out precisely. Both readings rest on the qadar of the previous verse.
Adh-Dhariyat closes a creation clause with the same praise formula: the earth We spread out, and excellent are those who spread. The construction states the act and then commends the actor.

links.why: everything created and then determined by a determining, the same root at full stretch

24.sense: The woe on the panel of the body. The evidence was taken from something every listener carries, so denial at this point is denial of what the denier is made of.

notes.t: The refrain has now closed three unlike kinds of evidence: the day named, the nations ruined, the person made. The sentence is not adjusted to fit any of them.
Al-Waqiʿa puts the creation argument in the opposite terms: We created you, so will you not hold it true. Tasdīq there is the exact contrary of the takdhīb named here.

25.sense: The third question. Kifāt is a vessel or a place that draws things in and holds them, from kafata, to gather up, to fold something in. The earth is described by what it does rather than by its size or its surface.

notes.t: Kafata is used of a bird folding its wings in and of a garment gathered at the waist. The noun names the place where that gathering happens.
Ta-Ha states the same double holding as a sequence: from it you were created, into it you are returned, and out of it you are brought a second time.

26.sense: Two words give the container its contents. The living are held on the surface, the dead inside it, and one noun covers both. Ground that already receives the dead is not being asked to do anything new.

notes.t: Ahyā'an and amwātan are accusatives depending on kifātan, so they name what the earth gathers rather than describing the earth itself.
Nuh puts it as a single sentence: Allah made you grow out of the earth, then returns you into it and brings you out again.

links.why: the same earth with its mountains blown off it, once the gathering is done

27.sense: The earth's description fills out. Rawāsī are anchors, from the root of a ship's mooring, and shāmikhāt are things that rise high, so the mountains hold and tower at once. Then the register drops from geology to a cup of water, and the address turns to ‘you’.

notes.t: Rāsiya is what is moored and does not drift; the same root gives mursā, a ship's anchorage in the story of Nuh. The word describes what the mountains do, not what they look like.
Furāt is fresh water that goes down easily. Al-Furqan sets it against milh ujāj, salt and bitter, the two kept apart by a barrier.
The mountains blown away at verse ten are the mountains planted here. The surah shows one object twice, once as a gift and once as something taken back.

links.why: the mountains cast into the earth so that it should not sway

28.sense: The woe on the panel of the earth. Mountains, height and drinkable water are given in a single verse, and the refrain answers what is done with them.

notes.t: The three questions opening with alam, did We not destroy and did We not create and did We not make, end at this refrain. What comes after it is no longer argument but the day itself.
Ya-Sin puts the same inference as a question with its answer attached: is the One who created the heavens and the earth not able to create their like. Yes, He is.

29.sense: The voice changes to a command given on the day itself. Intaliqū is the order to a party being moved off, and their destination is named only as the thing they denied. The refrain's verb has become the address they are sent to.

notes.t: The object is left unnamed. They are not sent to the fire by its name but to their own denial, handed back to them as a place.
As-Saffat gives the same movement as an order: gather those who wronged, and their kind, and what they used to serve, and drive them along the road to the blaze.

links.why: the day of decision named to them as the one they used to call a lie

30.sense: The order is repeated and given a direction. Zill is shade, the thing a traveller in that country moves toward, and the word arrives with all its relief attached. Then it is qualified: a shade with three forks, which is smoke standing in columns.

notes.t: Al-Waqiʿa gives the companions of the left a shade of black smoke, neither cool nor pleasant. The same trap is set there with the same noun.
Shuʿab are branches, the forks a road or a valley divides into. The number three is stated and not explained, and the early readings of it differ.

links.why: the shade the mindful are in, the same noun doing the opposite work

31.sense: The shade is taken back in the next breath. Zalīl is the intensive of zill, shade that actually shades, and it is denied outright. Two negations in a row remove first the comfort and then the protection.

notes.t: An-Nisa' promises the believers a zill zalīl, a deeply shading shade. The adjective denied here is the adjective granted there.
Abu Hurayra reported the Prophet ﷺ saying that the fire the son of Adam kindles in this world is one part of seventy parts of the fire of Hell.
notes.src: Bukhari, Book of the Beginning of Creation, and Muslim, Book of the Garden and its Description, from Abu Hurayra

notes.t: Lahab is the tongue of a flame, the reaching part that is visible. The verse says the smoke does not stand between them and it.

links.why: relief that is not relief, water like molten metal brought to those who call for help

32.sense: The fire is given a size by what comes off it. Sharar are the sparks that leap from a blaze, ordinarily small enough to brush away, and here each one is the bulk of a building. The comparison works by scale alone.

notes.t: Al-qasr is read as a fortified building, and also as qasar, the thick logs stacked for winter kindling. Reports from the early exegetes carry both, and the difference is one of vowelling.
notes.src: Bukhari records the explanation as stacked timber from Ibn ʿAbbas in his Book of Tafsir; at-Tabari carries both senses

notes.t: Tarmī is the verb for casting a stone or shooting an arrow: a throw with a direction, not a drift.

links.why: the same fire described from the inside rather than by what escapes it

33.sense: A second comparison laid over the first, for the same sparks. Size came from the fortress; movement and colour come from the camels, a train of them going together. The pronoun is singular and the noun plural, so the shower is seen as one body made of many.

notes.t: The Arabs called a dark camel sufr for the tawny cast in its black, so the colour word here can carry yellow and a burnt black at once.
Two similes for one thing, with no joining word between them: sparks like fortresses, then as though they were yellow camels. The second corrects the picture the first made rather than replacing it.

links.why: the same fire named lazā, described by what it strips rather than what it looks like

34.sense: The woe after the fire. Wayl was a word for ruin coming down on someone, and it is now said over people already being driven toward the smoke. The distance between the warning and the thing warned of has closed.

notes.t: The first four occurrences sealed arguments a listener could go and check. From here the refrain seals scenes, and the deniers it names are inside them rather than hearing about them.

35.sense: The scene goes quiet. Hādhā yawmu points at the day as though it were already present, and the clause that follows takes no object: they do not speak at all. Speech is the first thing removed, before any punishment is described.

notes.t: An-Naba' says none will speak except one whom the Merciful permits, and who says what is right. The silence is a withheld permission, which is what the next verse states.

The Qur'an elsewhere reports the deniers speaking on that day, swearing by Allah that they were never idolaters. The exegetes reconcile the two by reading the Day as having stations, speech allowed at some and not at others; others read this verse of a silence that falls at one particular point.
notes.src: compare 6:23; at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir both set out the reconciliation

links.why: mouths sealed and the hands and feet made to give the testimony instead

36.sense: The silence is explained. No leave is given, so the excusing never happens: the fā' makes the second verb a consequence that does not arrive. The reminder went out at the start of the surah to remove excuse; here the excuse has nowhere to go.

notes.t: Yaʿtadhirūn is from ʿ-dh-r, the root of ʿudhran at verse six. The two verses are the two ends of one argument: a warning sent so that no excuse would stand, and then no excuse admitted.
Ar-Rum says that on that day the excuse of the wrongdoers will not benefit them, and they will not be asked to make amends.

links.why: the same refusal, with the curse and the evil home named after it

37.sense: The woe after the silence. The panel it closes is two verses long: no speech, and then no leave to speak. The refrain is the only voice still working on the page.

notes.t: The refrain addresses nobody in the scene. Its grammar is a bare noun and two prepositional phrases, with no verb, no speaker named and no one spoken to.

38.sense: The naming returns. Yawm al-fasl was given at verse thirteen and left undefined at fourteen; here it is said again with the court assembled. The earliest peoples, destroyed at verse sixteen, are standing in the same gathering as the ones being addressed.

notes.t: Al-Waqiʿa states the same gathering: the former and the later, brought together for the appointment of a known day.
Three threads close in one verse: the day named at thirteen, the earlier peoples at sixteen, the appointment set at eleven. The surah has been assembling this sentence since its first section.

links.why: the earth laid bare and not one of them left out of the gathering

39.sense: A challenge put to the gathering. Kayd is a plan worked in secret against someone, which is what the deniers had been doing all along, and they are invited to do it now, in the open, against the one who gathered them. The final yā' of fa-kīdūni is dropped for the rhyme, leaving the nūn to close the verse.

notes.t: The same challenge is issued by prophets to their people: Hud telling them to scheme against him all together and grant him no respite, and the Prophet ﷺ told to say the like to those who call on their partners. Here it is not a prophet who says it.
At-Tariq answers the scheming directly and in the same words: they scheme a scheming, and I scheme a scheming.

40.sense: The woe after the challenge. Nothing comes back: the invitation to scheme is left with no reply in the text, and the refrain stands where an answer would go.

notes.t: Seven of the ten have now fallen, and each closed different ground: the day named, the ruined nations, the body, the earth, the fire, the silence, the challenge.

41.sense: The surah turns for the first time to the other party. Muttaqīn are those who keep a guard between themselves and what would harm them. They are put in zilāl, the plural of the very noun used for the smoke, and set beside water rather than fire.

notes.t: Zill at verse thirty was a shade that did not shade. The plural here comes without qualification, and the springs beside it settle what kind of shade is meant.
An-Nisa' promises a zill zalīl, a shade that shades, using the adjective this surah denied to the smoke.

links.why: extended shade and outpoured water given to the companions of the right

42.sense: The third thing given, after shade and water. Fawākih is fruit eaten for pleasure rather than for sustenance, and the clause ties it to their own wanting. What is provided is defined by the one receiving it.

notes.t: Az-Zukhruf makes the same provision general: in it is whatever the souls desire and the eyes take delight in.
Fākiha is distinguished in Arabic from the staple food. The word carries what is taken over and above need.

43.sense: The address turns to them directly, in the imperative. Hanī'an is food that goes down easily and leaves nothing behind it. The last clause attaches the meal to their own past work, so the eating is stated as a return rather than a gift.

notes.t: At-Tur has this sentence word for word, and Al-Haqqa gives it with a different ending: for what you sent ahead in the days now gone.
Hanī'an is used in An-Nisa' of a dower a wife gives up willingly, eaten with nothing owing on it. The word is about the absence of aftermath.

44.sense: The rule for the other party, cast in the shape of verse eighteen. Kadhālika nafʿalu bil-mujrimīn there, innā kadhālika najzī al-muhsinīn here. Ihsān is doing a thing well and beyond what is owed, set against jurm, the cutting of what should have held.

notes.t: As-Saffat closes the account of one prophet after another with this exact sentence, so the reward is stated as a standing practice rather than a single verdict.
Najzī is from jazā', the settling of an account. Kadhālika points back at the garden just described, and names it as the amount.

links.why: the matching sentence for the guilty, built on the same adverb

45.sense: The only occurrence that follows good news. The garden was described for four verses and then the same words return unchanged, so the deniers are placed here by what they are not given rather than by what they suffer.

notes.t: Every other occurrence closes a warning or a scene of punishment. Here the loss is the whole of the argument, and the wording is not adjusted to say so.
Al-Hashr states the same division flatly: the companions of the Fire and the companions of the Garden are not equal.

46.sense: The same imperative as verse forty-three, turned to the other party. Kulū is said to both, and everything after it differs: there, with relish, for what you did; here, a little, because of what you are. Qalīlan measures the whole of this world against the meal just described.

notes.t: Two commands to eat, three verses apart, addressed to opposite parties. This pairing is the surah's method throughout: one word given twice with its work reversed.
Luqman says the same plainly: We let them enjoy a little, then We force them to a harsh punishment.
Mujrimūn returns from verse eighteen, where the rule about the guilty was first stated. The sentence there is now read out to them.

links.why: brief enjoyment named for what it is, with the resting place after it

47.sense: The woe after the brief enjoyment. It follows a single verse this time, and that verse spoke to the deniers directly. The refrain goes back to speaking about them.

notes.t: The refrain never addresses the deniers. It is said over them in the third person, even here, where the line immediately before it used the second.

48.sense: The one verse in the surah about what the deniers do now rather than what will be done to them. Rukūʿ is the bowing of the prayer and stands for the whole of it. The refusal is put in the imperfect, a habit rather than one occasion.

notes.t: Al-Qalam says of the same people that they used to be called to prostrate while they were sound and able, and that on that day they will not be able to.
Umm al-Fadl bint al-Harith heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting Al-Mursalat in the Maghrib prayer, and said that after that he did not lead them in prayer again until Allah took him.
notes.src: Bukhari, Book of the Call to Prayer, and Muslim, from Umm al-Fadl bint al-Harith

notes.t: The verse arrives after the day has been shown from beginning to end. The last thing the surah describes is an ordinary refusal in an ordinary present.

49.sense: The tenth and last. It closes the shortest ground in the surah, one verse about bowing, and it ends the sequence with the words exactly as they stood at verse fifteen.

notes.t: Ten occurrences and no variation. Whatever the surah has just covered, whether evidence, history, the body, the earth, fire, silence, a challenge, a garden, a short enjoyment or a refusal to bow, the same three words close it.

50.sense: The surah ends on a question rather than a verdict. Hadīth is speech, an account given, and baʿdahu points back at the Qur'an they have just heard. If this has been called a lie, the question asks what is left that could be accepted.

notes.t: Al-Aʿraf ends a passage with these same four words, and Al-Jathiya asks it more fully: in what discourse after Allah and His signs will they believe.
The surah opened on an oath whose subject is never named and closes on a question that is never answered. The ayy of li-ayyi yawmin at verse twelve is the same particle as the fa-bi-ayyi here.

links.why: the surah's other open question, put about the day rather than about the speech
